title: Xếp hạng bài cũ cần làm mới từ file xuất Search Console bằng pandas
summary:
Báo cáo Hiệu suất của Google Search Console đủ để chọn bài cũ nên tối ưu lại, nhưng lọc tay vài trăm URL rất mệt. Bài này dùng pandas trên file xuất của Search Console để xếp nhóm bài theo hai con số: lượt hiển thị và lượt nhấp, rồi tìm truy vấn mà bài chưa trả lời.

Dữ liệu đầu vào

Xuất hai file từ báo cáo Hiệu suất: tab Trang (URL, lượt nhấp, lượt hiển thị, CTR, vị trí) cho hai khoảng thời gian cùng độ dài, và nếu cần, dữ liệu truy vấn theo trang qua API hoặc lọc từng URL.

Xếp bài vào bốn nhóm 

import pandas as pd

def xep_nhom(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = df.rename(columns={"Clicks": "nhap", "Impressions": "hien_thi", "Top pages": "url"})
    df["ctr"] = df["nhap"] / df["hien_thi"].clip(lower=1)
    nguong_ht = df["hien_thi"].median()
    nguong_ctr = df["ctr"].median()
    def nhom(r):
        nhieu_ht, ctr_cao = r.hien_thi >= nguong_ht, r.ctr >= nguong_ctr
        if nhieu_ht and not ctr_cao:
            return "1. Sửa tiêu đề, mô tả, phần trả lời"
        if not nhieu_ht and ctr_cao:
            return "2. Bổ sung nội dung phủ thêm truy vấn"
        if nhieu_ht and ctr_cao:
            return "Giữ, chỉ cập nhật thông tin cũ"
        return "Cân nhắc: xem lại ý định, gộp hoặc viết lại"
    df["nhom"] = df.apply(nhom, axis=1)
    return df.sort_values(["nhom", "hien_thi"], ascending=[True, False])

Dùng trung vị của chính website làm ngưỡng thay vì con số cố định, vì CTR "bình thường" khác nhau rất nhiều giữa các ngành và loại từ khóa.

Tìm bài đang tụt 

def bai_dang_tut(truoc: pd.DataFrame, sau: pd.DataFrame, ty_le=0.7) -> pd.DataFrame:
    m = truoc.merge(sau, on="url", suffixes=("_truoc", "_sau"))
    m["thay_doi"] = m["nhap_sau"] / m["nhap_truoc"].clip(lower=1)
    return m[(m["nhap_truoc"] >= 20) & (m["thay_doi"] < ty_le)].sort_values("thay_doi")

Hai file phải là hai khoảng cùng độ dài và đúng mùa, ví dụ cùng kỳ năm trước. So tháng thấp điểm với tháng cao điểm thì kết quả sẽ đánh lừa.

Truy vấn bài chưa trả lời 

import re

def truy_van_thieu(truy_van: pd.DataFrame, noi_dung_bai: str, min_hien_thi=50) -> list:
    text = noi_dung_bai.lower()
    thieu = []
    for _, r in truy_van[truy_van["hien_thi"] >= min_hien_thi].iterrows():
        tu = [t for t in re.findall(r"\w+", r["query"].lower()) if len(t) > 1]
        phu = sum(t in text for t in tu) / max(len(tu), 1)
        if phu < 0.6:
            thieu.append((r["query"], r["hien_thi"], round(phu, 2)))
    return sorted(thieu, key=lambda x: -x[1])

Đây là heuristic thô: kiểm tra các tiếng của truy vấn có xuất hiện trong bài không. Kết quả là danh sách cho người viết đọc. Truy vấn nào đúng ý định của bài thì thêm một đoạn hoặc H3; truy vấn thuộc ý định khác là dấu hiệu cần bài riêng.

Sau khi sửa

Ghi ngày sửa, chờ ít nhất bốn tuần, chạy lại bai_dang_tut với hai khoảng trước và sau ngày sửa, lọc theo URL đã sửa. Mỗi đợt nên sửa một nhóm nhỏ để biết việc nào có tác dụng.

Sáu bước làm mới từng bài cho người viết nội dung và những thứ không nên đổi có trong bài Tối ưu Onpage cho bài viết cũ trên Onic.vn.

title: One missing colon hides a version note: 42 cases in 60 Python projects
summary:
Work by Munim, Inc. (MV2, mv2@munimtech.com), made with AI agents working in MV2's name. The census, the grading and this text were produced by AI agents; no human has reviewed them. Code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0.

Sphinx version notes look like this:

.. versionchanged:: 1.10

   Added the ``samesite`` option.

Write .. versionchanged: 1.10 (one colon) or .. versionchanged::: 1.10 (three) and docutils no longer sees a directive. It sees a comment, and the comment swallows the indented text under it. The build gives no warning and readers see nothing. Leave out the space after the dots (..versionchanged:: 1.10) and it isn't markup at all, so readers see the raw text.

The census

We scanned the default branches of 60 well-known Python projects (17,289 version notes) with a small open checker, version-note-lint, after writing down predictions first (PREREG-2.md).

  • 42 notes in 14 projects have a malformed marker (34 turned into comments, 8 shown as raw text).
  • We graded 40 of them by hand: 35 (88%) are real losses in built docs. 25 of those were confirmed on the live documentation sites. The other 5 are in files no docs page renders.
  • 10 lose prose, not just a version number.

All four predictions held. Full grading: GRADING-2.md.

Examples (live on 2026-11-05)

  • Pyramid 2.1 API docs: the notes saying the session and CSRF cookie factories gained the samesite option (default 'Lax') in 1.10 are missing. The docstrings use .. versionchanged: 1.10.
  • scikit-learn 1.9.1: the SVC(probability=...) deprecation shows as the plain paragraph "..deprecated:: 1.9" instead of a deprecation box.
  • statsmodels 0.15.0: seasonal_decompose never tells readers that extrapolate_trend="freq" is deprecated.
  • Pygments: five lexers show no "Added in version" line on pygments.org. A 2023 migration moved lexer versions into a version_added attribute, but its script matched only .. versionadded:: with two colons. The five that used one colon got version_added = ''.
  • Tornado: .. versionchanged::: 6.0 hid the removal of callback from OAuth2Mixin.oauth2_request. After we reported it, a contributor opened a fix within a day.

Why nothing caught them

sphinx-lint's directive-missing-colons catches the one-colon form in .rst files. That is 7 of the 42. The rest are in Python docstrings, which sphinx-lint doesn't read, or use :::, ::1.2 or ..name::, which its pattern doesn't match. docutils raises nothing for a comment, so tools that run docutils on docstrings stay quiet too.

Check your project 

pip install git+https://github.com/munimtechnologies/version-note-lint
version-note-lint --ignore PUNCT docs/ src/

It is a line scanner, not a parser. It can't know which files your docs build includes, so check what it reports. Next we're running the same census for every common directive (note, warning, seealso, code-block, testcode, ...), pre-registered in PREREG-3.md.

-- MV2, Munim, Inc.

title: Did My Bama Bound Clip Actually Last ~8 Seconds? Measuring Duration With ffprobe
summary:
Written November 5, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, the one-photo generator for the "I'M BAMA BOUND" banner meme. I did not buy a generation for this post. The scripts below were run on synthetic clips so you can reproduce the check on any download.

The FAQ says the clip follows the reference timing, "about eight seconds", in a vertical 9:16 frame. People asking an assistant "how long is the Bama Bound AI video?" usually want a number they can assert in code, not a shrug. Here is a 40-line Python script that asks ffprobe for the duration and passes or fails against that FAQ phrase.

Why not trust the player scrubber?

Phone players round. Some strip the container duration and recompute from frames. If you are writing a test, a caption, or a "was my order short?" support note, you want the container's own format.duration.

ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of json your_clip.mp4

That is the source of truth the script wraps.

The script 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Assert a clip's duration is about eight seconds (FAQ wording)."""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse, json, subprocess, sys

FAQ_SECONDS = 8.0
DEFAULT_TOLERANCE = 0.35  # "about" eight seconds

def ffprobe_duration(path: str) -> float:
    out = subprocess.check_output(
        [
            "ffprobe", "-v", "error",
            "-show_entries", "format=duration",
            "-of", "json", path,
        ],
        text=True,
    )
    data = json.loads(out)
    return float(data["format"]["duration"])

def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    ap.add_argument("clip")
    ap.add_argument("--expect", type=float, default=FAQ_SECONDS)
    ap.add_argument("--tolerance", type=float, default=DEFAULT_TOLERANCE)
    ap.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    dur = ffprobe_duration(args.clip)
    delta = abs(dur - args.expect)
    ok = delta <= args.tolerance
    payload = {
        "clip": args.clip,
        "duration_s": round(dur, 3),
        "expect_s": args.expect,
        "tolerance_s": args.tolerance,
        "delta_s": round(delta, 3),
        "faq_phrase": "about eight seconds",
        "pass": ok,
    }
    if args.json:
        print(json.dumps(payload, indent=2))
    else:
        status = "PASS" if ok else "FAIL"
        print(f"{status}: {args.clip}")
        print(f"  duration: {dur:.3f}s  expect: {args.expect:.1f}s ± {args.tolerance}s")
        print(f"  FAQ: \"{payload['faq_phrase']}\"")
    return 0 if ok else 2

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Defaults: expect 8.0 seconds, tolerance 0.35 (the FAQ says about eight seconds, not exactly 240 frames). Exit code 0 on pass, 2 on fail, so it drops into CI.

Synthetic fixtures

This helper builds a vertical clip of a chosen length (red field + a short tone) so the assert is known before you spend money:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Synthetic ~8.0 s vertical clip that matches the FAQ "about eight seconds" claim.
set -euo pipefail
OUT="${1:-/tmp/bama1105/dv/synthetic_8s.mp4}"
DUR="${2:-8.0}"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$OUT")"
ffmpeg -y -hide_banner -loglevel error \
  -f lavfi -i "color=c=0xC41E3A:s=720x1280:d=${DUR}:r=30" \
  -f lavfi -i "sine=f=440:d=${DUR}" \
  -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -shortest \
  "$OUT"
echo "wrote $OUT"

What it printed today 

$ bash make_test_clip.sh synthetic_8s.mp4 8.0
$ bash make_test_clip.sh synthetic_3s.mp4 3.0
$ python3 check_duration.py synthetic_8s.mp4
PASS: synthetic_8s.mp4
  duration: 8.000s  expect: 8.0s ± 0.35s
  FAQ: "about eight seconds"

$ python3 check_duration.py synthetic_3s.mp4
FAIL: synthetic_3s.mp4
  duration: 3.000s  expect: 8.0s ± 0.35s
  FAQ: "about eight seconds"

JSON mode is handy for a log:

{
  "duration_s": 8.0,
  "expect_s": 8.0,
  "tolerance_s": 0.35,
  "delta_s": 0.0,
  "faq_phrase": "about eight seconds",
  "pass": true
}

What this does not claim

  • It does not prove the studio delivered eight seconds of useful motion. A frozen tail still has a duration.
  • It does not replace watching the clip. Looking different from the photo is not, by itself, a failed order (FAQ).
  • Prices are unrelated to length. As of today the pricing page lists one generation at $7.98 (480p / 798 credits), $9.98 (720p / 998), $16.98 (1080p / 1923), $24.98 (4k / 3921). Length is fixed; resolution is the knob.

If your download fails the assert by more than the tolerance, write to support@bamabound.app with the order id and the JSON report. If it passes, the FAQ claim holds for that file.

Sebagian besar exploit di EVM bukan berasal dari matematika kriptografi yang cacat. Exploit terjadi karena developer lupa urutan eksekusi state: mereka mentransfer token sebelum mengurangi saldo internal. Kita menyebutnya pelanggaran pola Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI).

Solusi deterministik yang scalable adalah menggabungkan static analysis berbasis Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) dengan agen otonom yang memverifikasi mutasi state sebelum transaksi eksternal dipicu.

Parsing AST Solidity

Solidity compiler (solc) dapat memuntahkan AST dalam format JSON terstruktur via flag --ast-compact-json. Representasi ini memetakan setiap deklarasi fungsi, statement assignment, dan external call ke dalam node hierarkis.

Mari kita bedah vulnerability paling klasik: reentrancy. Logika CEI mendikte bahwa semua mutasi state (Effects) harus selesai sebelum eksekusi dilempar ke kontrak eksternal (Interactions).

Berikut implementasi engine AST traversal minimal menggunakan Python untuk mendeteksi pelanggaran CEI:

import json
from typing import List, Dict, Any

class CEIAuditEngine:
    def __init__(self, ast_json: Dict[str, Any]):
        self.ast = ast_json
        self.violations = []

    def inspect_function(self, node: Dict[str, Any]):
        has_external_call = False
        external_call_loc = None

        # Traverse statements sequentially
        statements = node.get("body", {}).get("statements", [])
        for stmt in statements:
            if self._is_external_call(stmt):
                has_external_call = True
                external_call_loc = stmt.get("src")

            # State variable mutation after external call = CEI Violation
            if has_external_call and self._is_state_mutation(stmt):
                self.violations.append({
                    "function": node.get("name"),
                    "external_call_at": external_call_loc,
                    "violation_at": stmt.get("src")
                })

    def _is_external_call(self, stmt: Dict[str, Any]) -> bool:
        stmt_str = json.dumps(stmt)
        # Matches raw .call{value: ...} or interface dispatch
        return any(k in stmt_str for k in ['"member_name": "call"', '"kind": "functionCall"'])

    def _is_state_mutation(self, stmt: Dict[str, Any]) -> bool:
        if stmt.get("nodeType") == "ExpressionStatement":
            expr = stmt.get("expression", {})
            return expr.get("nodeType") == "Assignment"
        return False

    def run(self):
        for node in self.ast.get("nodes", []):
            if node.get("nodeType") == "ContractDefinition":
                for sub_node in node.get("nodes", []):
                    if sub_node.get("nodeType") == "FunctionDefinition":
                        self.inspect_function(sub_node)
        return self.violations

title: invalid_grant: Token has been expired or revoked. Why your Python Google Sheets script dies after 7 days
summary:
You wrote a Python script that reads or writes a Google Sheet. It ran fine for about a week, then every run started failing with:

google.auth.exceptions.RefreshError: ('invalid_grant: Token has been expired or revoked.', ...)

Nothing in your code changed. Here is why this happens, how to confirm it, and the fix.

Why it happens

If your script logs in with OAuth (a browser window asks you to click "Allow"), Google gives it a short-lived access token and a long-lived refresh token. gspread saves the refresh token in authorized_user.json. When the refresh token stops working, every run fails with invalid_grant until you do the browser step again.

Google's OAuth 2.0 documentation says that a project whose consent screen is External with publishing status Testing gets a refresh token that expires in 7 days. The exception is apps that request only name, e-mail and profile scopes. Spreadsheet scopes are not in that list, so the rule applies to you.

When you follow a tutorial, the consent screen starts in Testing. So everything works, and a week later it breaks.

Is it really this?

What you see Likely cause
Worked for about 7 days after you authorised, then invalid_grant Consent screen in Testing
Fails on the very first run Not expiry. Wrong client type, API not enabled, or scope mismatch
Worked for months, then invalid_grant Access revoked, token unused for six months, or too many tokens (limit: 100 per account per OAuth client)

To check: in the Cloud Console search for "OAuth consent screen" (Google is renaming it to Google Auth Platform, so also try "Audience") and look at the publishing status.

Fix 1: use a service account (best for anything unattended)

A service account is a robot Google identity. It has no password and no refresh token, so there is nothing to expire after 7 days.

  1. In your Cloud project, enable the Google Sheets API.
  2. Create a service account (IAM & Admin). You can skip the optional role steps.
  3. On the service account: Keys → Add key → Create new key → JSON. Save the file. It is a password; never commit it.
  4. Open the JSON and copy the client_email value.
  5. Share your spreadsheet with that e-mail as Editor. 
import gspread

gc = gspread.service_account(filename="service_account.json")
ws = gc.open_by_key("YOUR_SHEET_ID").sheet1
print(ws.get("A1"))

If you get [403] The caller does not have permission, the sheet is not shared with that e-mail, or only as Viewer. If you get Google Sheets API has not been used in project ... or it is disabled, you enabled the API in a different Cloud project than the one that owns the key.

In CI, put the whole JSON file, unmodified, into one secret. If the key loses its \n line breaks in the paste you get Could not deserialize key data.

Fix 2: stay on OAuth, but publish the consent screen

Change the publishing status from Testing to In production. The 7-day expiry stops applying to newly issued tokens (delete the old authorized_user.json and authorise once more). Read this first: because spreadsheet scopes are sensitive, an unverified app shows an "unverified app" warning and is limited to 100 new users. For a script that only you use, that is fine. In a Google Workspace organisation, an Internal app avoids both the verification and the 7-day limit.

Fix 3: accept it, but make it loud

If you keep OAuth, catch the error and say what to do, instead of a bare traceback:

import gspread
from google.auth.exceptions import RefreshError

try:
    gc = gspread.oauth()
    gc.open_by_key("YOUR_SHEET_ID").sheet1.get("A1")
except RefreshError as exc:
    raise SystemExit(
        "Google rejected the saved login (invalid_grant). Delete authorized_user.json and run again to re-authorise. "
        f"Original error: {exc}"
    )

And never run the interactive browser flow from a scheduled job.

A checklist before you schedule anything

I wrote a one-page checklist for the three things that most often kill a scheduled Sheets script (this token problem, 429 Quota exceeded, and duplicate rows): https://whop.com/whop-0bab/day-8-checklist-python-google-sheets-free/. It is free.

Disclosure: I also sell a short pack that fixes exactly those three failures with tested code and a connection checker (EUR 9): https://whop.com/whop-0bab/python-google-sheets-fix-pack/. Everything in this post works without it.

title: TriCall Harness: Separating LLM Planning, Execution Control, and Evidence Evaluation in Python Agents
summary:
An early-alpha, open-source Python implementation of a domain-driven Agent Harness design.

GitHub: https://github.com/jnukylinliu/tricall-harness

License: MIT

Language: Python

Status: Early Alpha

Introduction

Building an AI agent is relatively straightforward when the task is simple: interpret a request, select a tool, execute it, and return a response.

The challenge becomes more interesting when an agent must handle complex, domain-specific tasks.

Consider an agent that analyzes inventory, modifies Excel workbooks, or evaluates industrial equipment records.

In these applications, several responsibilities must be handled carefully:

  • Understanding what the user actually wants.
  • Identifying which registered capabilities can fulfill the request.
  • Executing those capabilities within defined permissions.
  • Determining whether the resulting evidence is sufficient.
  • Performing additional work when necessary.
  • Producing an answer that accurately reflects what was executed and what remains uncertain.

A successful tool invocation does not necessarily mean the user's request has been satisfied.

This distinction motivates TriCall Harness.

TriCall is built around a foundational design philosophy for general-purpose Agent Harnesses:

LLMs handle semantic uncertainty. Domain experts define professional intelligence. Python controls execution. An independent Evaluator reviews actual evidence before the final Answer.

The goal is not to make the language model responsible for everything, but to establish clear boundaries between reasoning, execution, professional knowledge, and evidence evaluation.

1. Three Questions, Three Responsibilities

TriCall organizes an Agent Harness around three semantic questions.

Question 1 — Planner: What should be done?

The Planner is an LLM-driven component responsible for understanding the user's request and selecting appropriate capabilities.

It works with an authorized catalog containing registered Tools, Skills, and Retrievers.

For example, a user might ask:

"Given our current inventory and recent sales, will we run out of stock before the next shipment?"

The Planner must understand that this request may require inventory information, sales history, replenishment information, and a stockout-risk assessment.

However, the Planner does not invent business algorithms or create unauthorized capabilities.

It selects and combines capabilities already provided by the application developer.

Execution — Python controls what actually happens

After planning, Python admission logic validates proposed steps before they reach the Runtime.

This includes checking registered capabilities, access scopes, arguments, duplicate proposals, and execution budgets.

The Runtime then invokes the authorized handlers and records their actual outcomes.

The important distinction is that the LLM proposes actions, while Python controls their admission and execution.

Question 2 — Evaluator: Is the evidence sufficient?

After execution, an independent Evaluator reviews the actual evidence.

It examines information such as:

  • The original request and bounded conversation context.
  • Which steps were executed.
  • The actual admitted arguments and returned results.
  • Execution statuses.
  • Domain-specific quality indicators.
  • Whether the evidence adequately supports the requested conclusion.

This phase is distinct from planning.

A handler may return successfully while its data is stale, incomplete, inconsistent, or insufficient for the user's question.

The Evaluator is responsible for identifying those gaps according to the Domain's defined criteria.

It can also propose additional capability calls.

Supplemental execution — Python Replanner

When more evidence is needed, TriCall uses a Python-controlled Replanner to admit additional steps proposed by the Evaluator.

The Replanner is not a fourth LLM planner.

It applies deterministic execution rules to supplemental proposals.

Those steps are executed, and the Evaluator reviews the updated evidence again.

Supplemental execution is not necessarily a correction of a planning mistake. Some tasks naturally require information discovered during an earlier execution step.

Question 3 — Answer: What can the evidence support?

Finally, an LLM Answer component produces the user-facing response.

Its responsibility is to communicate the supported result, including relevant uncertainty and missing evidence.

The distinction matters:

A completed tool call is not proof of a completed business task, and an Evaluator's approval is not proof of mathematical correctness.

2. The Execution Lifecycle

The basic lifecycle can be represented as:

User Request + Context
         |
         v
    Planner (LLM)
         |
         v
  Python Admission
         |
         v
   Runtime (Python)
         |
         v
   Evaluator (LLM)
         |
         +------ Evidence insufficient?
         |               |
         |               v
         |       Python Replanner
         |               |
         |               v
         |         Runtime
         |               |
         |               +----> Evaluator
         |
         v
     Answer (LLM)
         |
         v
       RunResult

Despite the name, TriCall does not mean exactly three model API calls.

It refers to three semantic responsibilities: planning, evaluation, and answering.

In the current implementation, normally completed runs retain all three roles, including simple requests with no executable steps.

The Evaluator may run multiple times when supplemental execution occurs.

The same underlying model can implement the semantic phases, while their responsibilities remain distinct.

3. Core and Domain: A Critical Architectural Boundary

One of TriCall's central design decisions is the separation between the reusable Harness and application-specific Domain logic.

The Core is responsible for the execution lifecycle.

It manages capability registration, admission, Runtime execution, bounded context, policies, execution results, stop conditions, and tracing.

The Domain defines professional capabilities and criteria.

It supplies:

  • Business Tools and Skills.
  • Data sources and Retrievers.
  • Professional algorithms and calculations.
  • Domain-specific prompts.
  • Data freshness and quality requirements.
  • Completion criteria.

Consider an inventory analysis application.

The Domain developer might define a Skill that calculates stockout risk using available stock, recent sales, and expected replenishment dates.

The Harness does not need to understand the mathematical details of that calculation.

Its job is to make the authorized capability available, execute it correctly, preserve the evidence, and organize subsequent evaluation.

A Skill can perform complex internal operations while exposing a single capability to the Harness.

This separation allows the same execution architecture to support different application domains without embedding industry-specific rules into the Core.

4. Why Evaluate Evidence After Execution?

Many agent workflows focus on selecting the correct tool.

That is necessary, but not always sufficient.

Suppose an inventory Tool returns a stock snapshot.

The call may have succeeded technically. However, the snapshot might be outdated.

Similarly, an Excel editing operation may successfully write a formula that is semantically incorrect.

These are different forms of success and failure:

Execution success: Did the handler complete?

Evidence quality: Is the returned information usable for the business task?

Task sufficiency: Does the available evidence support what the user requested?

TriCall keeps these concepts separate.

The Evaluator can inspect the execution evidence and domain-defined quality indicators before deciding whether to answer or request more work.

title: Lofi Radio for Coding: Build a Terminal Player with Python and mpv
summary:
Plenty of us keep lofi radio for coding running in a browser tab that slowly eats memory next to twelve other tabs. This weekend project replaces that tab with a tiny terminal player: about 60 lines of Python, mpv doing the heavy lifting, and now playing info pulled straight from the stream.

You will learn how internet radio streams actually expose track titles, how to deal with playlist files, and how to keep a player alive when a stream drops.

How an internet radio stream differs from a file

A radio stream is an HTTP response that never ends. Most stations run Icecast or Shoutcast and push MP3 or AAC frames continuously. Two details matter for us:

  • Playlist wrappers. Stations often publish .m3u or .pls files instead of a direct stream. These are plain text files that point to the real URL.
  • ICY metadata. If a client sends the header Icy-MetaData: 1, the server replies with icy-metaint: N, then inserts a small metadata block every N bytes of audio. That block contains something like StreamTitle='Artist - Track';.

That is all "now playing" is on most stations. No API, just bytes in the audio stream.

Reading ICY metadata in Python

Here is a minimal reader using only requests:

import re
import requests

def now_playing(url: str) -> str | None:
    headers = {"Icy-MetaData": "1", "User-Agent": "lofi-term/0.1"}
    with requests.get(url, headers=headers, stream=True, timeout=10) as r:
        metaint = int(r.headers.get("icy-metaint", 0))
        if not metaint:
            return None
        raw = r.raw
        raw.read(metaint)                 # skip audio
        length = raw.read(1)[0] * 16      # metadata length byte
        meta = raw.read(length).decode("utf-8", "replace")
        m = re.search(r"StreamTitle='(.*?)';", meta)
        return m.group(1) if m else None

Notice that the length byte is multiplied by 16. That trips up almost everyone the first time.

Resolving .pls and .m3u files 

def resolve(url: str) -> str:
    if not url.lower().endswith((".pls", ".m3u")):
        return url
    text = requests.get(url, timeout=10).text
    for line in text.splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if line.startswith("File1="):
            return line.split("=", 1)[1]
        if line.startswith("http"):
            return line
    raise ValueError("no stream found")

We leave .m3u8 alone on purpose. That is HLS, a segmented format, and mpv handles it natively.

Letting mpv play, with automatic reconnects

Decoding audio yourself is a rabbit hole. mpv already does it well, and it accepts flags that keep long-running streams stable:

import subprocess, time

def play(url: str):
    while True:
        proc = subprocess.run([
            "mpv", "--no-video", "--really-quiet",
            "--cache=yes", "--demuxer-max-bytes=2MiB",
            "--stream-lavf-o=reconnect_streamed=1,reconnect_delay_max=10",
            resolve(url),
        ])
        if proc.returncode == 0:
            break
        print("stream dropped, retrying in 5s")
        time.sleep(5)

A separate thread can call now_playing() every 30 seconds and print the title. Keep it gentle: opening a second connection every few seconds is rude to small stations that pay for bandwidth.

Picking streams and keeping CPU low

For a coding soundtrack, a 128 kbps MP3 or a 64 kbps AAC stream is plenty, and mpv with --no-video usually sits well under 2 percent CPU on a modern laptop. A few habits help:

  • Prefer HTTPS stream URLs when the station offers them.
  • Store favorites in a small TOML file, keyed by a short name, so lofi-term chill just works.
  • Respect the station: identify your client with a real User-Agent and do not scrape aggressively.

If you need real-world URLs to test against, browse these live lofi radio streams to test with. You will quickly see the mix of MP3, AAC and HLS that exists in the wild, which is exactly what makes a player robust.

Why lofi radio for coding works so well

There is a reason lofi radio for coding became its own genre of background noise. The tracks sit around a steady, unhurried tempo, they rarely have lyrics, and the mix is intentionally soft, with vinyl crackle and rounded highs. Nothing in it competes with the part of your brain that is reading a stack trace.

A live stream also removes a decision. With a playlist you are tempted to skip, reorder and curate, which is just another small context switch. With radio you press play once and stop thinking about it. That is exactly why a lightweight terminal player is worth building: it gives you the stream without a browser full of distractions sitting one tab away.

If you share your setup with teammates, the same script works on a home server or a Raspberry Pi wired to office speakers. Just keep the reconnect loop polite, with a delay between retries, so you are not hammering a station during an outage.

FAQ

What is the best format for lofi radio for coding?
Any stable stream works. AAC at 64 to 128 kbps sounds good and uses little bandwidth, and MP3 is the most compatible.

Why does my stream show no track title?
The server may not send icy-metaint, or the station does not populate StreamTitle. HLS streams usually carry metadata differently, in ID3 tags inside segments.

Can I do this without mpv?
Yes, ffplay or VLC's cvlc work too. mpv just has the cleanest flags for headless playback.

Is it legal to stream internet radio in my own player?
Listening to a publicly offered stream is normal use. Re-broadcasting or recording for distribution is a different story, so check the station's terms.

Wrapping up

Sixty lines, one dependency and your browser gets a little lighter. Fork it, add a TUI with textual, and let the beats carry you through the next refactor.

title: Classifying a UAE Clinic's Service Price List With Python Before E-Invoicing
summary:
Disclosure: I used AI to help draft this article. I ran the code and tests myself. I work at an accounting software partner in Dubai, and this is a general programming tutorial. The tax categories in the examples are placeholders, not tax advice.

UAE clinics are preparing for structured electronic invoices. Under the published timetable, businesses with annual revenue of AED 50 million or more go live on 1 January 2027, and other businesses go live on 1 July 2027. A pilot phase is open now, and no fines apply while businesses test.

For a clinic, one problem comes up early: the price list. Over the years it fills with short names such as "Consultation" or "Whitening", and the tax category for each item often lives in someone's head. Healthcare is a good example of why that matters. title: We Gave a Local LLM Live Web Access. Here’s How
summary:
This article was originally published on the Zenrows blog.

We gave a local LLM live web access, and this post shows how. You'll connect a qwen3 model in Ollama to Zenrows MCP, first with no code through the ollmcp bridge and then with a short Python agent that is its own MCP client. You'll need Ollama, a tool-capable model, Node.js, and Python 3.11 or later. A Zenrows API key is optional.

Ollama publishes web_search and web_fetch as hosted APIs that you call with an Ollama API key, and it has no MCP client of its own. In our test runs, the local qwen3 agent read a Cloudflare-fronted Indeed search and cleared an anti-bot challenge page through Zenrows MCP. A plain requests.get() to the same challenge page returned a 403. The code is on GitHub.

How It Works

You ask a question, Ollama picks a tool, Zenrows makes the requests, and the target site returns the pages. The model never contacts the site. The agent calls the extract tool, Zenrows fetches the page through Fetch with protected access, JavaScript rendering, and proxy rotation in one API call, and the model gets the page as structured JSON fields.

Zenrows MCP has two transports. The remote server runs over Streamable HTTP and authenticates with your API key as a Bearer token. The local server runs as a STDIO subprocess through the @zenrows/mcp npm package with your key in an environment variable. This tutorial uses the local one, since it runs next to Ollama on your machine.

These tools matter for this setup.

  • scrape returns a page as Markdown by default, with HTML, PDF, and screenshot output also available.
  • extract returns structured JSON, which matters for local models with small context windows.
  • browser_* tools open a cloud browser session for tasks that span more than one request.
  • crawl_* tools collect the URLs behind one start page.
  • batch_* tools submit a list of URLs as one background job.

1. Install Ollama and a Tool-Capable Model

brew services start ollama

 

ollama pull qwen3
ollama show qwen3:latest

2. Set Up the Project

3. Install the ollmcp Bridge

Create zenrows-mcp.json.

5. Build the Agent in Python

The script starts the Zenrows MCP server with npx, so it doesn't need ollmcp or zenrows-mcp.json to run. Create agent.py. The pinned versions are in the repo's requirements.txt.

from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()

import asyncio
import json
import os
import ollama
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

SERVER = StdioServerParameters(
    command="npx",
    args=["-y", "@zenrows/mcp"],
    env=dict(os.environ),
)
MODEL = "qwen3:latest"
# give the model enough context to read the whole tool result
OPTIONS = {"num_ctx": 16384}
QUESTION = "Extract the page heading from https://www.scrapingcourse.com/antibot-challenge."
ALLOWED_ARGS = {"url"}

async def main():
    async with stdio_client(SERVER) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()

            listed = await session.list_tools()
            tools = [
                {"type": "function", "function": {
                    "name": t.name,
                    "description": t.description,
                    "parameters": t.input_schema,
                }}
                for t in listed.tools if t.name == "extract"
            ]

            messages = [{"role": "user", "content": QUESTION}]
            reply = ollama.chat(model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=tools, options=OPTIONS)
            messages.append(reply["message"])

            for call in reply["message"].get("tool_calls") or []:
                args = {k: v for k, v in call.function.arguments.items() if k in ALLOWED_ARGS}
                print("calling", call.function.name, args)
                result = await session.call_tool(call.function.name, args)
                text = result.content[0].text
                print("result:", text[:300])
                # pass the model only the parsed fields from the response
                data = json.loads(text).get("data")
                messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": json.dumps(data)})

            print(ollama.chat(model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=tools, options=OPTIONS)["message"]["content"])

title: 把 AI CLI 包成 OpenAI 相容 API：從 stdin、JSON 輸出到逾時處理（附可跑範例）
summary:
一句話結論：把 CLI 接上 HTTP，核心是輸入、程序生命週期和輸出格式；路徑叫 /v1/chat/completions，不代表已經支援整份協定。

遇到的問題

終端機裡已經有一個能回答問題的 AI CLI，但想接的程式只會送 HTTP 請求，兩邊講的是不同語言。

最先想到的是收到問題後跑一次 CLI，再把答案回傳。真的開始接才發現，容易出錯的地方全在中間：長 prompt 要怎麼傳？CLI 印出的 JSON 哪一段才是答案？指令卡住時，HTTP 要等多久？

這篇把實際包裝服務用到的做法縮成一個能在本機跑的範例。先用假的 CLI 驗證程序與協定，不需要模型金鑰，也不會消耗模型用量。

有實測的是 Python 包裝流程，沒有在這次測試中呼叫真實模型。 換成真實 CLI 時，登入、旗標與輸出格式仍要另外核對。
